evals.name: unique-email-with-release
evals.prompt: In a C# Chronicle app, `UserRegistered(EmailAddress Email, DisplayName Name)` must keep Email unique across all users, with the message 'Email already registered.', and `UserRemoved` must free the email again. Write both event types. Give the code in your reply; do not write files.
evals.expected_output: Property-level [Unique] with an explicit name and message passed by name on the Email parameter, and [RemoveConstraint] with the exact same name on UserRemoved.
assertions: Puts [Unique] on the Email property (property-level), not on the class, because the value must be unique across event sources.
Passes the attribute arguments by name (name: ..., message: ...) and gives an explicit name.
Marks UserRemoved with [RemoveConstraint] using exactly the same name string as the [Unique] name.

evals.name: case-insensitive-iconstraint
evals.prompt: Project names must be unique case-insensitively, and ProjectRemoved releases the name. A developer wrote `.On<ProjectRegistered>(e => e.Name.ToLower())` inside an IConstraint. Explain what happens and give the corrected constraint. Reply with code.
evals.expected_output: CHR0020 rejects a method call in the lambda; suppressing it leads to PropertyDoesNotExistOnEventType at startup. Use On<ProjectRegistered>(e => e.Name).IgnoreCasing().RemovedWith<ProjectRemoved>().
assertions: States the lambda is a method call rather than a pure member-access chain and is rejected by analyzer CHR0020.
States that suppressing the analyzer fails at startup with PropertyDoesNotExistOnEventType.
Uses .On<ProjectRegistered>(e => e.Name).IgnoreCasing() instead of lowercasing in the lambda.
Uses .RemovedWith<ProjectRemoved>() on the fluent builder to release the claim.

evals.name: violation-is-a-result
evals.prompt: Write the EventScenario specification proving a second `ProjectRegistered("Acme")` append is rejected by the project name constraint, and say how the violation is surfaced to the caller and what to assert. Give the code in your reply; do not write files.
evals.expected_output: Seed with Given, append again, assert failure and ShouldHaveConstraintViolationFor the constraint name; the violation comes back on the append result, not as an exception, and message text is not asserted by default.
assertions: Seeds the conflicting state through the scenario's Given and appends the duplicate through the scenario's event log.
Asserts ShouldBeFailed and ShouldHaveConstraintViolationFor with the constraint name.
States that a violation comes back on the append result (HasConstraintViolations, ConstraintViolations) and is not thrown as an exception.
Does not assert the message text by default, since presentation text can change without behavior changing.

evals.name: constraint-boundaries
evals.prompt: A team wants a Chronicle constraint to enforce 'at most 10 bookings per boat' and also thinks the command's pre-check 'does the registration number exist?' is enough against concurrent requests. What do you tell them about what constraints can and cannot do? Reply only.
evals.expected_output: Constraints give append-time uniqueness/create-once that holds when requests race, but cannot count, sum or test predicates; capacity needs a decision read, stream decision or aggregate; a command pre-check reads possibly stale state.
assertions: States that a constraint cannot count, sum or test a predicate, so a capacity rule needs a decision read, a stream decision or an aggregate.
States that a command-side pre-check reads state that may be stale by the time the append lands, whereas a constraint is evaluated inside the append.
States that uniqueness is the right use of a constraint and it binds every writer.
